title: Failing Silently vs. Reporting Errors
objective: Decide when an except block should fail silently with pass and when it should report the error instead.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only; the file-handling part of this book chapter is covered separately in Code Forge's Files chapter. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Catching an exception doesn't force you to print anything about it. The pass statement is a no-op — it does nothing at all — so except SomeError: pass catches the error and lets the program continue as if that one case simply didn't happen. This is called failing silently.

Failing silently is useful when an error is expected and harmless to ignore, such as skipping a file in a batch that happens to be missing an optional field. But overusing it hides real bugs: if something breaks and no message ever appears, you can spend a long time guessing why the program behaves oddly.

The alternative is to report the error — print a message, log it, or show the user something went wrong — even while keeping the program running. As a default, prefer reporting: it costs little, and it turns silent, mysterious failures into visible ones you can actually fix.
explanation.rule: Default to reporting an error you catch; reach for pass only when the failure is expected and truly doesn't need anyone's attention.

examples.title: Silent vs. Reported Lookups
examples.note: silent_lookup gives no clue that "carol" was missing — it just returns None. reported_lookup prints a message first, so the cause is visible before the None appears.

checks.question: Which situation is the best fit for using pass in an except block?
options: An expected, harmless case where ignoring the error is genuinely fine.
A bug in your own code that you haven't investigated yet.
Any exception, since pass keeps the program running no matter what.
An error the user needs to know about before continuing.

feedback.correct: Correct — pass fits expected, harmless cases; unexplained bugs should be reported, not hidden.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. pass is appropriate for errors you've deliberately decided are fine to ignore, not for bugs or errors the user needs to see.

assignment.title: Count Valid Ages
assignment.brief: Write count_valid_ages(entries) that takes a list of text values, tries to convert each to an int, and returns how many converted successfully. For values that fail to convert, print a warning message and skip them instead of failing silently.
requirements: Use try/except ValueError around int(entry) for each one.
On failure, print a message naming the bad entry (don't use pass) and continue to the next entry.
Return the count of entries that converted successfully.
assignment.starterCode:
def count_valid_ages(entries):
    # Return how many entries in the list convert to a valid int.
    # Print a message for any entry that fails to convert.
    pass

requirementChecks.label: Does not fail silently with pass

assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    print(count_valid_ages(["25", "thirty", "41", ""]))
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.expectedOutput:
Skipping invalid age: thirty
Skipping invalid age: 
2
assignment.outputCheckLabel: Prints a skip message for "thirty" and for the empty string, then prints 2 as the final count

hints: Loop over entries with a for loop, and put the try/except inside the loop body.
int(entry) belongs inside try — that's the line that can raise ValueError.
Instead of pass in the except block, print a message that includes the bad entry.
Use an else block (or a line after the try/except) to increment your counter only when the conversion succeeded.
An empty string "" also fails int() conversion and should be reported just like "thirty".
